consigne: Here are six messages received this morning. For each one, decide whether to report it or whether it is legitimate. Use the “Check the link” button to see where a link really leads. Nothing is sent: this is a simulation.

messages.objet: Action required: your password expires today
messages.corps:
Dear user,

Your password expires in **2 hours**. Without action on your part, access to your mailbox will be suspended.

Click the link below to keep your current password.
indices: Sender address outside the {{organisation.domaine}} domain
Urgency and threat of suspension
Generic greeting “Dear user”
The link leads to verif-compte.co, not to {{organisation.domaine}}
messages.explication: Classic phishing: a real IT department never asks you to “keep” your password through a link.

messages.objet: Reminder: enter your summer leave before 30 April
messages.corps:
Hello everyone,

To organise schedules, please enter your summer leave requests on the intranet before 30 April.

The HR team
indices: Internal sender with the right domain
Usual request, without excessive urgency
The link really leads to the organisation's intranet
No request for a password or payment
messages.explication: Legitimate message: consistent sender and link, expected request. Even here, when in doubt, you can open the intranet from your bookmarks rather than the link.

messages.corps: Your parcel could not be delivered. Redelivery fee: €1.99. Pay within 48h:
indices: Unknown phone number
Small amount to obtain your bank details
Short deadline to rush you
Website belonging to no known carrier
messages.explication: Smishing: the small amount is used to steal your card number. Carriers do not ask for fees by text message.

messages.objet: Reactivate your two-factor authentication before Friday
messages.corps:
A security update requires you to reactivate your two-factor authentication.

Scan the QR code below with your phone to complete the procedure.
indices: Sender domain unrelated to the provider
QR code in an email: it escapes security filters
Forces you to use a phone, often less protected
Deadline to rush you
messages.explication: Quishing: the QR code hides the fake website's address. Two-factor authentication is managed only through the official tools provided by {{organisation.nom}}.

messages.objet: Wave of fake delivery text messages: stay alert
messages.corps:
Hello,

Several colleagues received fake delivery text messages this morning asking for €1.99. Don't click and report them.

Thank you to those who have already reported them: thanks to you we were able to react.

The security team
indices: Sender: the official security contact
No link, no attachment, no risky request
Informative message consistent with current events
messages.explication: Legitimate message: it informs without asking for anything sensitive. An alert asking you to click or enter a password would, on the other hand, be suspicious.

messages.corps: “Pay for your parking online: scan me!” The QR code is printed on a sticker placed over the town hall's official poster.

qrCode.description: QR code on an added sticker

indices: Sticker added over the official display
Address unrelated to the town or the official operator
Request for card payment
messages.explication: Physical quishing, common on parking meters and charging stations. Use the official app or website you know.
